comparison: Both evaluations support the core findings of BCG-induced protection and myeloid population changes (C1, C2, C4). OpenEval additionally includes C3 (CM-T identification via scRNA-seq) which peer reviewers address separately. Both find the CFU and flow cytometry data convincing.

Both support elevated STAT1/Ly6a expression (C5, C6) and CM-T identification (C3, C9). OpenEval also includes literature-based mechanistic claims (C7, C8) which peer reviewers group with other literature citations. Peer reviewers explicitly highlight CM-T identification as a novel strength.

OpenEval supports CCR2 downregulation findings (C9, C10). Peer reviewers acknowledge this as part of the broader CM-T characterization without specific concerns, treating it as contributing to the novel cell population identification.

Both address BCG localization (C12, C13). OpenEval finds the data well-supported and notes it challenges prior bone marrow localization requirements. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, suggesting BCG persistence in spleen may have unresolved mechanistic implications for the tissue-specific phenotype.

Both support the temporal dynamics of training signatures (C14-C19). OpenEval emphasizes distinct kinetics between transient CM-T and persistent SCA-1+ NCM populations. Peer reviewers praise the kinetics characterization and accept the correlation between waning CM-T and reduced protection without challenge.

OpenEval supports RPM training signatures (C20, C21). Peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader temporal dynamics and myeloid population shifts, noting the work defines kinetics across multiple populations including RPM.

Both strongly support the temporal transcriptional profiling (C22-C24, C29-C31). OpenEval details specific gene kinetics and biphasic STAT1 dynamics. Peer reviewers specifically praise the in-depth temporal transcriptome investigation as a main strength of the study.

OpenEval supports gene function claims (C25-C27) as appropriate integration of expression data with literature. Peer reviewers group these literature-based contextual claims together and accept them without challenge, indicating they provide helpful context.

OpenEval supports IRG1 temporal expression and mechanistic inference (C28). Peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader temporal transcriptional profiling without specific concerns about the transient expression pattern.

OpenEval rates heme metabolism enrichment (C32) and RPM repopulation link (C33) as UNCERTAIN, noting the connection is speculative. Peer reviewers group C33 with other literature citations and accept without explicit challenge, though they don't specifically validate this inference.

Perfect agreement on bone marrow transplant findings (C34, C35). Both evaluations support that progenitor programming contributes to SCA-1+ NCM persistence but not CM-T. Peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating progenitor contribution to training.

Both support lineage tracing findings (C36-C38). OpenEval details the MS4A3 reporter data showing BM-derived RPM contribution. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the demonstration of RPM replenishment from recruited monocytes as a key advance.

Both support differential gene expression across cell types (C39-C42) and literature-based gene functions (C43, C44). OpenEval emphasizes clustering patterns. Peer reviewers accept the transcriptional characterization of replenished cells as part of the dual-route mechanism.

Both support training in BM-derived and tissue-resident RPM (C45-C48). OpenEval notes quantitative differences in response magnitude. Peer reviewers emphasize this dual contribution as demonstrating long-term protection depends on resident cells.

Both support the dual-route model synthesis (C49). OpenEval treats this as well-supported by converging evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly state this shows protection is dependent on resident cells, treating it as a key advance.

Both support STAT1-KO findings (C50, C51). OpenEval notes the mechanism of RPM depletion isn't directly tested. Peer reviewers accept STAT1 requirement for myeloid population changes as part of the broader STAT1-dependent response demonstration.

Both support JAK inhibitor findings (C52-C55). OpenEval emphasizes differential effects of Fedratinib vs Deucravacitinib demonstrating IFNγ-JAK2-STAT1 specificity. Peer reviewers accept this as revealing STAT1-dependent responses are required for training.

Both support Fedratinib blocking of training phenotypes (C56-C60). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive phenotypic characterization. Peer reviewers accept this as linking the trained immunity phenotype with early STAT1 activation through IFNγ.

Both support gene set enrichment showing IFNγ response as top affected pathway (C61). OpenEval notes consistency with STAT1-regulated program. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the STAT1-dependent response characterization.

Both support α-IFNγ blocking experiments (C62, C63). OpenEval emphasizes this demonstrates IFNγ signaling rather than BCG presence is critical. Peer reviewers accept this as complementing the inhibitor studies showing STAT1 requirement.

Both support the critical early window finding (C64). OpenEval notes transient early inhibition is sufficient to block training. Peer reviewers accept this as part of demonstrating STAT1-dependent responses are required for training establishment.

Both address trans-acting signaling (C65, C66). OpenEval supports the inference based on absence of BCG in BM plus LSK+ expansion. Peer reviewers rate this UNCERTAIN, noting the contrast with previous BCG-in-BM models and suggesting BCG persistence in spleen may be mechanistically important.

Both address STAT1's central role synthesis (C67). OpenEval finds this well-supported by comprehensive evidence. Peer reviewers accept STAT1 requirement but express uncertainty about the trans-acting mechanism interpretation versus local BCG persistence effects.

Both support background claims about cell lifespan and training duration (C68-C71). OpenEval treats these as establishing conceptual framework. Peer reviewers accept the framing without challenge as appropriate context.

Both support background claims about BCG training mechanisms (C72-C76). OpenEval treats these as establishing prior understanding of BM progenitor reprogramming. Peer reviewers accept these as appropriate background context.

Both support background claims about tissue-resident macrophages (C77-C81). OpenEval treats these as context for investigating RPM training. Peer reviewers accept these as appropriate background without challenge.

Both support the summary conclusions (C82-C85). OpenEval finds these well-supported by comprehensive evidence. Peer reviewers affirm the work advances understanding of tissue-resident cell contributions to trained immunity, accepting the overall conclusions.
